opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it. The first is just control. If you're building a product where the model is the core of what you deliver, depending entirely on someone else's API means your roadmap, your costs, and even your quality are tied to decisions you don't make. Teams want to be able to change the architecture, retrain on their own data, fix a failure mode the day they find it, instead of waiting and hoping a provider addresses it.

The second is that "AI" isn't one problem. A general-purpose language model is amazing, but if you work on something like physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, or video generation for simulation, your data looks different, your evaluation metrics are different, and the constraints on latency and compute are different. A model tuned for chatting isn't automatically good at understanding how objects move in 3D space or how light behaves in a scene. So in many domains you have to build your own, because what you need doesn't exist yet.

The third reason is about learning. Training a model yourself, even a smaller one, teaches the team things you can't get by reading papers or calling an endpoint: how the data pipeline really behaves, where scaling breaks, which tricks actually matter. That knowledge compounds. Organizations that have gone through the full loop of data, training, evaluation, and deployment tend to move much faster on the next iteration.

And honestly, there's a strategic and even emotional element. Researchers want to push the frontier, and companies see foundation models as core infrastructure, like owning your own engine instead of buying one. Not everyone needs to do it, and I think we'll see some consolidation, but as long as the field is moving this quickly and the problems are this diverse, you'll see many teams building their own models.

r001.rationale: The response discusses control, domain needs, learning, and strategic motivation, but does not say interpersonal disagreements lead people to leave existing AI organizations to build models.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute constraints, but does not identify buying computing power or sufficient funding as an enabler of independent model development.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think it comes down to a few things, and they're not all about technology.

The first is control. When you build on someone else's model, you inherit their decisions: what data went in, what behaviors were tuned out, what the model is and isn't allowed to do. That's fine if your product is close to the center of what the model was built for. But if you're doing something specific, say simulation for robotics, or video generation for a particular industry, the general-purpose model is often not quite right, and you can't reach inside and fix it. Owning the model means you own the whole stack of decisions.

The second is that the knowledge is in the building, not the using. Training a frontier model teaches you things you simply can't learn from an API. You learn where the data bottlenecks are, what the scaling behavior looks like, which architectural choices actually matter. Teams that only consume models end up one step removed from the real understanding, and in a field moving this fast that's a dangerous place to be.

The third is strategic. Nobody wants their core business sitting on top of a dependency that another company can reprice, restrict, or shut off. If AI is the heart of what you do, renting the heart feels uncomfortable.

And then honestly, the fourth is culture. Researchers want to build. Give a strong team compute and a hard problem, and they will want to train their own thing. That ambition is part of why the field advances so quickly.

So there's duplication, yes, and not every team should be doing this. But I don't think it's irrational. Most of these teams are making a bet that the differentiation of their product will ultimately live in the model, and if they're right, they need to own it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses control, strategic independence, and researchers’ ambition, but does not say interpersonal disagreements cause people to leave existing AI organizations to build models.

r002.rationale: It says a strong team given compute may want to train its own model, but does not identify buying computing power or sufficient funding as the enabler.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few reasons. One is that people have different ideas about what a model should be good at. A team might care about coding, another about visual understanding, another about running efficiently. Building your own model gives you control over those trade-offs.

There’s also a strategic reason. If the model is central to your product, you may want control over its capabilities, its cost, and how it evolves. You don’t want your entire roadmap to depend on someone else’s decisions.

But that doesn’t mean every team needs to train a model from scratch. The important question is: what can you do differently? If you have unique data, a different technical approach, or a specific problem that existing models don’t solve well, there’s a clear motivation. Otherwise, building on an existing model can be a very good choice.

r001.rationale: The response mentions teams having different ideas about model priorities, but does not say interpersonal disagreements cause people to leave existing AI organizations to develop their own models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses control over cost and capabilities, but does not identify buying computing power or sufficient funding as an enabler of independent model development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few reasons. First, teams have different goals, and building your own model gives you more control over what you optimize for. You might care about a particular capability, efficiency, or how the model fits into your product. Second, there’s a learning aspect. When you train a model yourself, you develop knowledge that’s hard to get just by using somebody else’s API.

But I don’t think every team needs its own foundation model. The question is whether owning that part of the technology creates enough value to justify the investment. Sometimes it does; sometimes you can accomplish much more by building on an existing model.

r001.rationale: The response mentions teams having different goals, but does not say interpersonal disagreements lead people to leave existing AI organizations and develop their own models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses training a model and investing in one, but does not identify buying computing power or sufficient funding as an enabler.
